title: Time value of money
objectives: Answer out loud: Why is $1 today worth more than $1 tomorrow?
Answer out loud: What happens to the PV of a 20-year cash flow if rates rise?
Answer out loud: What does the discount rate represent?

steps.body: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar later because you can invest today's dollar and earn a return.
Future value: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n. $100 at 10% for 2 years = $121.
Present value runs it backwards: PV = FV / (1 + r)^n. $121 in 2 years at 10% = $100 today.
The discount rate is the return you *give up* by not investing elsewhere at similar risk — your opportunity cost.
Higher discount rate → lower present value. Further-out cash flows → hit harder by the discount rate.

legend.meaning: Present value — what the cash is worth today
Future value — what it grows to

blocks.prompt: PV of $110 received in 1 year at a 10% discount rate → **?**
blocks.solution: PV of $110 received in 1 year at a 10% discount rate → $100

blocks.title: Why is the discount rate called a "required return" and not an "interest rate"?
blocks.teaser: An interest rate is what a lender charges.
blocks.body:
An interest rate is what a lender charges. A required return is what *any* investor needs to earn to accept a given level of risk. For a risky business, that's far above a bank interest rate. In valuation, the discount rate always reflects the risk of the cash flows being discounted.

**Interview answer:** "The discount rate is the return investors require for the risk they're taking — their opportunity cost — so riskier cash flows get a higher rate and a lower present value."

blocks.title: Why are long-dated cash flows more sensitive to the discount rate?
blocks.body:
The rate compounds. Moving from 8% to 10% barely changes the PV of a cash flow next year (0.926 → 0.909), but cuts the PV of a cash flow in 20 years by about a third (0.215 → 0.149). This is why growth companies — whose value sits far in the future — fall harder when interest rates rise.

**Interview answer:** "Discounting compounds, so a rate change hits distant cash flows much harder. That's why long-duration assets like growth stocks are most rate-sensitive."

blocks.prompt: Rates rise from 8% to 10%. Which cash flow's present value falls the most in percentage terms?

options.text: They all fall by the same percentage

blocks.explanation: Discounting compounds, so distant cash flows are hit hardest: the 20-year factor drops from 0.215 to 0.149 (about a third), while next year's barely moves (0.926 → 0.909).

blocks.title: Nominal vs. real — why must cash flows and rates match?
blocks.teaser: Nominal figures include inflation; real figures strip it out.
blocks.body:
Nominal figures include inflation; real figures strip it out. If you project nominal cash flows (with price increases) but discount at a real rate, you overstate value. Mixing them is a consistency error, the same family as using EV/Net Income.

**Interview answer:** "Nominal cash flows get a nominal discount rate, real get real. Mismatching them inflates or deflates the value."

blocks.title: Does compounding frequency matter?
blocks.teaser: Yes — more frequent compounding means slightly more growth.
blocks.body: Yes — more frequent compounding means slightly more growth. 10% compounded annually turns $100 into $110; compounded monthly, about $110.47. Interviews rarely test the math, but you should know why a monthly-compounding loan costs more than its stated annual rate.
